name: Eoraptor
fact: One of the very FIRST dinosaurs, 231 million years ago! It was small (like a medium dog), fast, and probably ate anything it could catch. All dinosaurs — every single one — came after creatures like this.

name: Plateosaurus
fact: One of the first BIG plant-eating dinosaurs. It could rear up on its hind legs to reach high branches like a living giraffe. Shows how quickly dinosaurs started experimenting with getting large.

name: Ichthyosaurs
fact: NOT a dinosaur — a reptile that went BACK into the sea and re-evolved into a dolphin shape! Evolution independently invented the streamlined swimmer body at least twice. They gave birth to live young in the water.

name: Eudimorphodon
fact: One of the first pterosaurs — the very first vertebrates to achieve powered flight! Not birds, not bats. Pterosaurs figured it out first, 228 million years ago. They were NOT dinosaurs but lived alongside them.

name: Early Mammal (Morganucodon)
fact: The first true mammals — tiny, shrew-like creatures that mostly hid from dinosaurs and came out at night. For 150 MILLION YEARS, our mammal ancestors were small and stayed out of sight. Patient little survivors.

name: Nothosaurus
fact: A marine reptile with a long flexible spine and sharp teeth. Could fold its flippers against its body for speed. Not a dinosaur or ichthyosaur but another marine reptile. The Triassic seas were crowded!

name: Cynodont
fact: A small mammal-like synapsid with fur and whiskers! Getting closer to true mammals. They had specialized teeth and ears optimized for night hunting. The direct ancestors of all living mammals including you!

name: Coelophysis
fact: One of the earliest theropod dinosaurs - a pack-hunting speedster built like a greyhound with hollow bones. Mass death sites in New Mexico preserve hundreds of individuals together suggesting they traveled in groups. NASA even sent a Coelophysis skull to the Mir Space Station in 1998.
know: At Ghost Ranch, New Mexico, a single quarry opened in 1947 holds the skeletons of hundreds of Coelophysis that died together. A Coelophysis skull was carried to the Mir space station in 1998.

name: Postosuchus
fact: A rauisuchian - a crocodile cousin that stood fully upright and dominated the Triassic landscape before dinosaurs rose to prominence. With its massive skull and serrated teeth, Postosuchus was the T. rex of its day. It shows that dinosaurs did not immediately take over after the Permian extinction.

name: Tanystropheus
fact: A spectacularly bizarre reptile with a neck longer than its body and tail combined - held stiff by only 13 elongated vertebrae. Recent studies show it came in two forms: juveniles lived on land eating insects, adults lived in the sea catching fish.

name: Proganochelys
fact: The earliest well-known turtle, and it already had a complete shell but couldn't retract its head. The turtle body plan has been so successful it has not fundamentally changed in over 200 million years.

name: Shonisaurus
fact: The largest ichthyosaur ever discovered - as long as a sperm whale. Its fossils were found in the Nevada desert which was once open ocean. Unlike later ichthyosaurs Shonisaurus had teeth only at the front of its jaws, suggesting it grabbed squid-like prey with a quick snap.

name: Nyasasaurus
fact: Either the oldest dinosaur known or the closest thing to one — 10 to 15 million years older than any other. It is known from one upper-arm bone and six vertebrae that sat in a museum drawer for decades after being collected in the 1930s.
know: Thin slices of the arm bone show tissue laid down fast and without pause — the rapid growth that marks dinosaurs. A crest on the bone for powerful shoulder muscles is found only in dinosaurs.
debate: With so little of the skeleton, it cannot yet be placed firmly inside or just outside Dinosauria.

name: Herrerasaurus
fact: One of the first big meat-eating dinosaurs, with a sliding joint in its lower jaw that let it flex around struggling prey. It is named for Victorino Herrera, the goat-herder who led scientists to the bones in 1959.
know: Layers of volcanic ash above and below the fossils contain crystals that can be dated by radioactive decay, pinning these earliest dinosaurs to about 231 million years ago.

name: Staurikosaurus
fact: A slim, fast hunter from the very dawn of dinosaurs. It was named for the Southern Cross constellation because, when it was described in 1970, dinosaurs from the Southern Hemisphere were still a rarity.

name: Riojasaurus
fact: A long-necked plant-eater that was already bigger than an elephant while most dinosaurs were still dog-sized — an early step on the road to the giant sauropods.

name: Ingentia
fact: Described in 2018, Ingentia shows that dinosaurs reached giant size about 30 million years earlier than anyone thought — and by a different route from later sauropods.
know: Its bones have thick growth rings, like a tree: it grew in huge seasonal spurts rather than steadily. Hollows in its neck bones held bird-like air sacs that kept so large a body cool.
sites: Balde de Leyes, San Juan, Argentina

name: Liliensternus
means: Named for Hugo Rühle von Lilienstern, a doctor and amateur fossil hunter
fact: The top predator of Late Triassic Europe: light, long-legged and probably a hunter of Plateosaurus, whose herds lived on the same plains.

name: Thecodontosaurus
fact: The “Bristol dinosaur”, found in 1834 and one of the first half-dozen dinosaurs ever named. It lived on limestone islands in a warm shallow sea, and its bones washed into caves and cracks in the rock.
know: Much of the original material was destroyed when Bristol's museum was bombed in 1940. New finds in a nearby quarry in 1975 gave scientists thousands of bones to work on again.

name: Eodromaeus
fact: A small, fast hunter from the dawn of dinosaurs. Its name means “dawn runner”.

name: Tawa
fact: An early meat-eater from New Mexico whose bones suggest the first dinosaurs spread out from South America.

name: Silesaurus
fact: A close cousin of the dinosaurs with a beak at the front of its jaw.
know: Fossil dung thought to be from Silesaurus is packed with beetles — one of them a species new to science, described from the droppings in 2021.

name: Saurosuchus
fact: The top predator of the earliest dinosaurs' world. In the Triassic, the crocodile line — not dinosaurs — ruled.

name: Desmatosuchus
fact: An armoured plant-eater from the crocodile line, with long spikes jutting from its shoulders and a pig-like snout for rooting.

name: Effigia
fact: A crocodile relative that walked on two legs and had a toothless beak — it looks like an ostrich dinosaur, 80 million years before those existed.
know: Collected in 1947, it sat in plaster jackets at the American Museum of Natural History until a student opened them in 2004.

name: Hyperodapedon
fact: A barrel-bodied, beaked plant-eater — the commonest animal in the rocks where the first dinosaurs are found.

name: Erythrosuchus
fact: One of the first big predators after the Great Dying, with a huge head.

name: Euparkeria
fact: A small, agile animal close to the common ancestor of crocodiles, dinosaurs and birds.

name: Thrinaxodon
fact: A burrowing mammal relative that survived the Great Dying.
know: An X-ray scan in 2013 found a Thrinaxodon curled up in its burrow beside an injured amphibian — two different animals sheltering together.

name: Placerias
fact: A heavy, tusked plant-eater the size of a cow. At one quarry in Arizona, about 40 were found together.

name: Mastodonsaurus
fact: A giant flat-headed amphibian. Two tusks in its lower jaw were so long they poked through holes in the top of its snout.

name: Cymbospondylus
fact: One of the first true giants. A skull 2 m long, described in 2021, shows a whale-sized predator just three million years after the Great Dying.

name: Mixosaurus
fact: A small early ichthyosaur, already shaped like a dolphin but with a less powerful tail.

name: Placodus
fact: A sea reptile with flat, crushing teeth for cracking clams and snails pried off the seabed.

name: Henodus
fact: It looks like a turtle, with a wide, flat shell — but it is a placodont, not a turtle. Its square mouth may have strained food from the mud.

name: Atopodentatus
fact: A sea reptile with a hammer-shaped head and needle teeth like a zip — for scraping algae off rocks and sieving it out.

name: Sharovipteryx
fact: A tiny glider with its wing membrane stretched between its very long hind legs — the opposite of a bat or a pterosaur.

name: Proterosuchus
fact: A crocodile-like hunter with a hooked upper jaw, one of the first archosaurs — the group that later included crocodiles, pterosaurs, dinosaurs and birds.

name: Cynognathus
fact: A wolf-sized hunter from the mammal line, with dog-like teeth.
know: Its fossils in South America, Africa and Antarctica — continents now separated by ocean — were among the clues Alfred Wegener used to argue that continents move.

name: Kannemeyeria
fact: A big, tusked, beaked plant-eater — one of the dicynodonts that spread across the world after the Great Dying.

name: Chaohusaurus
fact: The oldest known ichthyosaur. One fossil was caught giving birth — the baby coming out head-first, as land animals are born.
know: Ichthyosaurs later gave birth tail-first, like whales, so the baby would not drown. A head-first birth suggests their ancestors had only recently left the land (2014).

name: Hupehsuchus
fact: A toothless, armoured sea reptile with a long, narrow snout.
debate: A 2023 study argued it filter-fed like a baleen whale, with a stretchy throat and soft tissue in place of teeth — but no baleen has been found.

name: Keichousaurus
fact: A small, long-necked sea reptile that gave birth to live young. So many have been found in Guizhou that they are sold in rock shops worldwide.

name: Asilisaurus
fact: An early cousin of the dinosaurs, 10 million years older than the oldest dinosaur. It shows the dinosaur branch split off earlier than anyone thought.

name: Teleocrater
fact: One of the oldest members of the bird line — yet it walked on four legs like a crocodile (2017). The upright, two-legged stance came later.

name: Ctenosauriscus
fact: A sail-backed reptile from the crocodile side of the family — evidence that the archosaurs had already diversified within five million years of the Great Dying.

name: Galesaurus
fact: A cynodont of the hard years after the Great Dying. Adults have been found curled up with youngsters — signs of parents caring for their young 250 million years ago.

name: Bauria
fact: A therocephalian that evolved broad, grinding cheek teeth and a bony palate just as the cynodonts did — the same mammal-like answers, reached separately.

name: Diademodon
fact: A pig-sized cynodont with wide cheek teeth that met tooth-to-tooth for grinding plants — proper chewing, a mammal habit.

name: Trirachodon
fact: A burrower. Tunnel systems in South Africa hold up to twenty skeletons together: the oldest known colony of land animals living in a shared burrow.

name: Massetognathus
fact: A plant-eater the size of a small dog, and one of the most common animals in its world — the rabbits of the Triassic.

name: Exaeretodon
fact: A big plant-eating cynodont that lived beside the very first dinosaurs — and at first far outnumbered them.

name: Lisowicia
size: About 4.5 m; as heavy as an elephant
fact: The last and largest dicynodont: an elephant-sized mammal cousin living among early dinosaurs. Unlike its sprawling relatives it stood on upright legs, like a rhino.
know: Found in a clay pit in Poland in 2006 and named in 2019. Its size showed that dinosaurs were not the only animals becoming giants in the Late Triassic.

name: Brasilodon
fact: A mouse-sized insect-eater, very close to the start of mammals. Its jaws show it grew just two sets of teeth — baby teeth, then adult teeth — as we do.
debate: A 2022 study argued that two sets of teeth mean it fed its young on milk, pushing mammal-style life back to 225 million years ago. Not everyone agrees the teeth prove that.

name: Parasuchus
fact: It looks like a crocodile but is not one: the nostrils sit on a bump right in front of the eyes, not at the tip of the snout. The same shape evolved twice for the same river-ambush life.
know: Two skeletons from India were found with the bones of small reptiles in their stomachs.

name: Paracyclotosaurus
fact: A giant amphibian shaped like a flat-headed crocodile. It probably lay still in the shallows and opened its huge mouth so fast that fish were sucked in.
